evidence: Cic. Att. 5.14.2: adventus noster nēminī nē minimō quidem fuit sūmptuī
Caes. BG 1.18.5: suō sūmptū, at his own expense
Traupman 311: meō sūmptū, at my expense
terms.comment: The everyday word, in the singular or the plural (Lewis & Short). At my expense, meō sūmptū; to go to expense, sūmptum facere; to spare no expense, sūmptū nōn parcere (Cic. Fam. 16.4.2, see spend). To be a cost to someone is sūmptuī esse alicui.

terms.gloss: outlay, cost (money laid out on something)
evidence: Cic. Att. 13.25.3: quoniam impēnsam fēcimus in macrocola (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Properly money laid out (pecūnia understood, from impendere, to spend): impēnsam facere in rem, to spend money on a thing.
Mostly in the plural (Lewis & Short). In Cicero’s letters it is also the interest paid on a loan (faenus et impendium, Att. 6.1.4), so say sūmptus where that could mislead.

phrases.latin: nūllus sūmptus est, et sī sūmptus esset, tamen valētūdinis causā experīrēs
phrases.english: it costs nothing, and even if there were an expense, you would still try it for your health

phrases.latin: adventus noster nēminī nē minimō quidem fuit sūmptuī
phrases.english: my arrival did not cost anyone a penny

phrases.latin: vēneram in suburbānum meum et querēbar dē impēnsīs aedificiī dīlābentis
phrases.english: I had come out to my place outside town and was complaining about the cost of the crumbling building

sources: Lewis & Short: sumptus · Lewis & Short: impendo · Lewis & Short: impendium (impēnsa is given under impendō)
